# qd-cache source

Keeps a local SQLite copy of what the app fetched from GitHub (pull requests, lists, changed files, stacks and combined diffs), so a launch shows the last known review queue before the network answers and the app stays usable offline, and the UI state it restores after a relaunch. It owns the schema and its migrations. It does not fetch anything and does not decide when data is stale beyond comparing a pull request's `updated_at` and the commits a file set was fetched for; the app refreshes and writes back.

Smart filters are user state, like paid-for briefs: typed tables store each review scope's latest plan, generation time, head and base SHA, ordered buckets, ordered review items with guidance and exact member paths. Legacy bucket membership migrates to one item per file. The Files navigation mode is persisted with the review layout. Replacements are transactional. Cache cleanup never deletes these plans.

Guided review generation reserves a typed `guided_review_runs` row per scope. Publication takes the SQLite writer lock, checks the run identity and head/base revision, then claims the host's cancellation gate immediately before replacing the complete guide. The same transaction saves its validation receipt, run and snapshot identities, cost, session, model, duration, and up to 512 ordered tool audit events with up to 64 issue codes each. Exact retries recover the current durable receipt without rewriting it. A stale generation, accepted cancellation or failed child-row write leaves the prior guide and metadata unchanged. Drafts, MCP capabilities, raw answers and transcripts are never persisted.

Briefs use an independent generation reservation and the same publication metadata contract. Their pages, widgets, existing run record, receipt, captured comparison base and typed audit commit together. Both captured commits must match the reservation; the restored base also identifies base-only changes in a combined review. Legacy saved briefs have no MCP receipt and remain readable. Reading a brief holds one SQLite snapshot across its artifact and metadata so another process cannot attach a newer receipt to older pages. The in-session `BriefRecord` still owns raw artifact output and transcript; database restore leaves those fields absent.
